Photios I was patriarch of Constantinople twice, from 858 to 867 and from 877 to 886, and the leading scholar of his age. Born around 815 into a rich family that had suffered for supporting icons, he was a palace official and teacher when Emperor Michael III raised him, a layman, to patriarch within days, in place of the deposed Ignatius.

Pope Nicholas I refused to accept him, and the quarrel became the Photian schism. In 867 Photios held a council that condemned the pope and attacked the Western addition of the Filioque to the creed. When Basil I seized power that year he deposed Photios, but later brought him back. Leo VI removed him for good in 886.

He backed the mission of Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs, and his Bibliotheca sums up 279 books he had read, many now lost. The Orthodox church honours him as Saint Photios the Great.
